list.listitem: While guidelines recommend that patients with type 1 DM (T1DM) for > 5 years and all patients with type 2 DM (T2DM) be screened annually for albuminuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), evidence that this reduces the risk of end-stage renal disease is lacking. C
In patients with diabetes, intensive glycemic control (HbA1c < 7%) may delay or prevent development of micoalbuminuria and myocardial infarction, but adverse effects are uncertain. B
In patients with diabetes and hypertension, lower blood pressure targets (SBP <120 vs <140, or DBP <80 vs <90) have unclear benefits in preventing end-stage renal disease (ESRD). B
In patients with diabetes with or without hypertension, angiontensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE) prevent the onset of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) and decrease mortality. B
In patients with DKD, ACE or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) may prevent progression to ESRD. B
In patients with T2DM and DKD, sodium-glucose co-transporter protein 2 inhibitors (SGLT2) reduce the progression of DKD and decrease cardiovascular and all-cause mortality. A

background.definition: Diabetic nephropathy, also known as diabetic kidney disease (DKD), is a microvascular complication of T1DM or T2DM. It is diagnosed as presence of persistent albuminuria (urinary albumin/creatinine ratio ≥30mg/g) or reduced eGFR (<60 mL/min/1.73m2) for at least 3 months. However, loss of kidney function (reduced eGFR) may progress without albuminuria.

list.listitem: DKD occurs in 20-40% of patients with diabetes.

Overall, the prevalance of DKD has not changed significantly (ie, 28.4% in 1988-1994, versus 26.2% in 2009-2014). The prevalance of albuminuria decreased from 20.8% in 1988-1994 to 15.9% in 2009-2014. However, the prevalance of reduced eGFR increased from 9.2% in 1988-1994 to 14.1% in 2009-2014.
In 2009-2014, 8.2 million adults with diabetes had albuminuria, reduced eGFR, or both.

2017 Medicare expeditures for diabetics and chronic kidney disease (CKD) in >65 years of age at initial and then subsequent yearly cost for nephropathy was $9,576 and $1,875; for ESRD on dialysis was $54,739 and $38,622; and for ESRD treated by transplant was $79,859 and $15,568.
DKD is the most common cause of ESRD in the United States (at least 45% of patients with kidney failure).
DKD markedly increases cardiovascular risks and all-cause mortality.

There are care gaps in prescribing SGLT2 and renin angiotensin blockade for DKD, and especially disparities noted by age, non-white race, females, and low income persons or Medicare recipients. Cost of SLGT2 may be a barrier, as well as clinician oversight in screening.
T1 or T2DM
Glomerular hyperfiltration is felt to be an early manifestation of disease, and also likely contributes to accelerated loss of kidney function.
Hyperglycemia and accumulation of advanced glycosylation end-products in the glomeruli contribute to glomerular injury.

A variety of proteins, cytokines and growth factors have been implicated in the pathogenesis and proposed as biomarkers of DKD, but there is still lack of clarity about the implication of these for therapeutic targets.

Guidelines recommend that patients with type 1 DM for >5 years and all patients with type 2 DM be screened annually for microalbuminuria and with a GFR estimate; however, direct evidence that this improves patient-oriented outcomes is lacking. C
If detected, albuminuria is confirmed by its presence in at least 2 of 3 specimens over 3-6 months and by the absence of a urinary tract infection. C
In patients with diabetes, intensive glycemic control (HbA1c < 7%) may delay or prevent development of micoalbuminuria and myocardial infarction, but adverse effects are uncertain. B
In patients with diabetes and hypertension, lower blood pressure targets (SBP < 120 vs <140, or DBP <80 vs <90) have unclear benefits in preventing end-stage renal disease (ESRD). B
In patients with diabetes with or without hypertension, angiontensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE) prevent the onset of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) and decrease mortality. B
The coexistence of retinopathy and proteinuric kidney disease in diabetes is virtually diagnostic of diabetic nephropathy and usually does not require kidney biopsy. C
Atypical features of DKD such as macroalbuminuria in absence of retinopathy or rapid loss of kidney function should prompt investigation into other causes and may require kidney biopsy. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Higher degree of proteinuria, severe hypertension, rapid loss of kidney function
Consider if atypical features present (absence of retinopathy, severe proteinuria)
Features of systemic lupus: rash, photosensitivity, arthritis, positive serology for lupus
Abrupt onset of nephrotic syndrome, younger age
Abrupt increase of creatinine of at least 50% after initiating ACE or ARB
Rising creatinine due to relative hypoperfusion secondary to underlying condition

list.listitem: Early DKD is unlikely to be manifest on history and physical exam. Patient is likely to have at least a 5 year history of DM if type 1, but is at risk for DKD at time of diagnosis if type 2. Hypertension is very common in diabetics with kidney disease.
Retinopathy is strongly correlated with development of diabetic nephropathy.

Patients with advanced kidney disease and heavy proteinuria may have significant edema. Symptoms of uremia such as fatigue, sleep disturbance, nausea, itching and metallic taste are suggestive of very advanced kidney disease.

The American Diabetes Association Standards of Care 2024 and the KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guidelines both recommend using the urinary albumin/creatinine ratio (ACR) and the estimated glomerular filtrate rate (eGFR) to assess for DKD. Microalbuminuria is defined as ACR of 30 to 300mg/g, while macroalbuminuria is ACR >300 mg/g. Reduced GFR is <60 mL/min/1.73m2.

Measurement of a random spot urinary ACR is a reliable way of detecting microalbuminuria, and can also be used to follow patients with known albuminuria to track progression of disease. Timed urine collections such as 8 and 24 hour collections for measurement of albuminuria tend to be less reliable and more burdensome for patients. Assessment of proteinuria by chemstrip (urine dip) is capable of detecting macroalbuminuria, but not microalbuminuria, and is not recommended as a screening test.

The modification of diet in renal disease (MDRD) equation provides reliable and reproducible GFR estimates in patients with impaired kidney function (GFR <60) but is less reliable in patients with normal or near-normal kidney function. The Cockcroft-Gault equation also provides reasonable estimates but is somewhat less reliable than MDRD in patients with impaired kidney function. The National Kidney Foundation currently recommends use of the CKD-EPI 2021 calculator to calculate eGFR; cystatin C can optionally be added to this formula for increased GFR accuracy.
Kidney biopsy can provide definitive evidence of DKD, but is usually not necessary except in atypical cases.
See for a suggested approach to diabetic nephropathy.

All patients with diabetes and DKD should be treated with a comprehensive plan to optimize nutrition, exercise, smoking cessation, and weight, including medications to preserve organ function (especially heart and kidneys) and reach targets for glycemia, BP and lipids.
For patients with DKD, angiontensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE) or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) may prevent progression to ESRD. B
For patients with DKD, metformin has uncertain benefits in preventing the progression of DKD. B
For patients with T2DM and DKD, sodium-glucose co-transporter protein 2 inhibitors (SGLT2) reduce the progression of DKD and decrease cardiovascular and all-cause mortality. A

For patients with T2DM and DKD when additional glycemic control is needed, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP1) may reduce progression of DKD, as well as reduce cardiovascular and all-cause mortality. B

For patients with T2DM and DKD on SGLT2 and maximally tolerated ACE or ARB but with ongoing albuminuria, nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (nsMRA) may reduce progression of DKD and cardiovascular events. B
For patients with DKD, treatment with an ACE or ARB may prevent progression to ESRD.

The best studied agents for reducing albuminuria and slowing progression of GFR decline in patients with established DKD (macroalbuminuria and/or decreased GFR) are ACE and ARB. The mechanisms of action for ACE and ARB are similar, and either class of medication is efficacious for patients with diabetic microalbuminuria and hypertension.

For patients with macroalbuminuria and decreased GFR (overt nephropathy), ACE may slow progression in T1DM, while ARB may be effective for T2DM. There have been no large head-to-head comparisons of the two classes in overt nephropathy. DKD guidelines suggest that ACE and ARB are likely to be equally efficacious for T1DM or T2DM with overt nephropathy.

For patients with DKD and HTN needing further BP control, thiazide diuretics and/or dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers may be used in combination therapy in a regimen already containing an ACE or ARB.

On initiating ACE or ARB, a rise in creatinine up to 30% from baseline should be accepted and not confused with an acute kidney injury. The combination of ACE plus ARB, or either ACE/ARB plus direct renin antagonist (aliskiren), may be associated with increased adverse events and should be avoided.

Steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (sMRA), may potentiate the action of ACE to reduce proteinuria. Before more strongly recommended, this effect will need to be determined in studies of longer duration. Also, concerns of dual renin angiotensin aldosterone system blockade and hyperkalemia exist.

A meta-analysis of three RCTs of sodium-glucose co-transporter protein 2 inhibitors (SGLT2) suggested that they may reduce the risk of progression of renal disease in patients with T2DM, with similar effects in participants with or without ASCVD.
A 2024 Cochrane meta-analysis showed that SGLT2 in DKD decreased kidney disease, as well as cardiovascular and all-cause death.

A KDOQI 2023 commentary on the KDIGO 2022 guidelines highlights significant new trials showing strong evidence for the renal and cardiac benefit of certain SGLT2 (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, sotagliflozin, empagliflozin) and GLP1 (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, efpeglenatide), as well as evidence for nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (finerenone) in reducing progression of DKD.

A 2024 meta-analysis evaluated the effects of combining SGLT2, GLP1, and nsMRA together, showing improvements in major adverse cardiovascular events (hazard ratio 0.65, (95% CI, 0.55-0.76), with an estimated absolute risk reduction of 4.4% over 3 years, and number needed to treat of 23. This combo of meds also showed improvements in heart failure hospitalizations, chronic kidney disease progression, cardiovascular death, and all-cause death.

Treatment of hyperlipidemia with statin therapy targeting LDL-C levels less than 100 mg/dl may reduce cardiovascular risk in patients with DKD; this benefit does not appear to extend to patients with end stage renal failure on dialysis.

Excellent glycemic control early in the course of T1 and T2DM reduces the onset and progression of microalbuminuria. While this reduces the risk of progression of microalbuminuria to macroalbuminuria, a meta-analysis and the ACCORD, ADVANCE and VA Diabetes trials found either no macrovascular benefit or an increased risk of all-cause mortality in patients targeting a glycosylated hemoglobin <6.0% or 6.5% compared with a target of 7.0% to 7.9%. Higher goals are more appropriate in patients with limited life expectancy, established diabetic complications, longstanding diabetes mellitus or increased risk of hypoglycemia. Individualized Hba1c targets should be made and sought for patients with DKD based on safety; KDIGO 2022 recommends <6.5 to <8%, and ADA 2024 recommends <7%.

BP control is recommended to help reduce cardiovascular risks that are associated with DKD. Overly aggressive BP targets have been associated with adverse events. Individualized BP targets should be made and sought for patients with DKD based on safety; KDIGO 2022 recommends systolic BP <120, and ADA 2024 recommends BP <130/80 (consistent with ACC/AHA 2017 target).

In patients with diabetes and hypertension, lower blood pressure targets (SBP < 120 vs <140, or DBP <80 vs <90) have unclear benefits in preventing end-stage renal disease (ESRD), based on a Cochrane review.

Diets that adhere to the USRDA for protein intake (0.8 g/kg body weight per day) may reduce albuminuria and stabilize DKD. High protein diets may worsen albuminuria and accelerate progression of kidney disease. However, a Cochrane review found unclear benefits for dietary protein restriction in altering the progression of DKD.

Diets lower in sodium intake may potentiate the effect of ARB to limit GFR decline in DKD. Limiting salt intake to less than 5g per day (2g sodium) helps lower BP in DM (regardless of HTN or DKD). KDIGO 2022 recommends limiting sodium to <2g per day, and ADA 2024 recommends <2.3g per day.

High-dose B vitamins increased adverse cardiovascular outcomes and all-cause mortality in a randomized trial of 238 adults with diabetes type 1 or type 2 and chronic renal failure. A Cochrane reviewfound no evidence to substantiate vitamin B therapy to treat DKD.
A systematic review of 9 RCTs of vitamin D supplementation found no significant effects on the progression of albuminuria.
Based on a Cochrane review, intensive educational programs and behavioral counseling appear to improve glycemic control in patients with DKD but have uncertain effects on patient-oriented outcomes.
Patients with evidence of overt DKD (macroalbuminuria and/or GFR below 60 ml/min) should be referred to a nephrologist for co-management.
Patients with significant hyperkalemia should be treated urgently to prevent cardiac arrythmias.
Patients with an acute and rapid deterioration in kidney function should be evaluated urgently or hospitalized for further management.

Patients with progressive kidney failure may need initiation of renal replacement therapy or referral for kidney transplant once uremic symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, itchiness, fatigue or metallic taste of food develop.

A patient who develops hyperkalemia or rapid decline in kidney function (>30% from baseline) following initiation with or an increase in ACE or ARB dose should have the medication held temporarily, and later resumed at a lower dose if previously tolerated.
Patients who develop cough from an ACE should be changed to an ARB.
Patients who are unable to tolerate either an ACE or ARB because of side effects or hyperkalemia should be treated with a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker or thiazide.
Volume status (risk of dehydration) should be monitored while on SLGT2.
If treatment is initiated at the microalbuminuria stage, progression to macroalbuminuria can be prevented or delayed. B
The presence of microalbuminuria or macroalbuminuria is associated with increased cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. B

Although patients with persistent microalbuminuria have an increased risk of development of DKD, they do not always progress. In one case-control study, more diabetic patients without microalbuminuria progressed to overt nephropathy (17% vs 6%).
Over a 10 year period, 30% of T1DM with microalbuminuria will progress to overt nephropathy; and up to 40% of T2DM with microalbuminuria will progress.
Once at the reduced GFR stage, most patients will inevitably lose GFR at a rate of 10-20 ml/min per year and ultimately develop ESRD.
In both T1DM and T2DM, GFR may decline in the absence of progressive albuminuria.

Patients with DKD are at increased risk of cardiovascular death. In prior eras, patients with DKD would frequently die prematurely before progressing to ESRD. In the current era, more patients with DKD reach ESRD than die prematurely from cardiovascular disease.
Treating at the microalbuminuria stage reduces progression to macroalbuminuria.
Once a patient is at the macroalbuminuria or reduced GFR stage, treatment slows the progression of DKD, but is not able to reverse or cure it.

Risk models developed from the ADVANCE trial found strong associations between baseline eGFR and urinary ACR and major kidney-related events (doubling of serum creatinine, need for dialysis, death from renal causes).
Microalbuminuria and overt proteinuria confer a substantial increase in risk for cardiovascular events and mortality.
Patients with microalbuminuria should continue to have assessment of microalbumin levels annually to look for progression of albuminuria.
Serum creatinine should be followed annually in patients with GFR >60 ml/min, every 6 months in patients with GFR 45-60 ml/min, and every 3 months in patients with GFR <45 ml/min.
For GFR <60, patients should be monitored regularly for BP, volume status or fluid retention, electrolyte abnormalities, anemia metabolic acidisis, and metabolic bone disease.

Patients with DKD are also at substantially increased cardiovascular risk, and should have annual monitoring of lipid profiles along with aggressive treatment of hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and risk factor optimization.
Patients contemplating pregnancy or actively trying to conceive should be taken off ACE or ARB therapy.

ACE and ARB are contraindicated in pregnancy and should be discontinued immediately when pregnancy is suspected or confirmed. Instead, consider beta blockers and calcium channel blockers as they appear to prevent the risks of severe hypertension among pregnant women with mild to moderate hypertension.

All pregnant patients with underlying kidney disease are at increased risk for hypertension in pregnancy, pre-term delivery and pre-eclampsia; patients with pre-conception serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dl or higher are also at risk for worsening kidney function. Ideally this information should be offered during pre-conception counseling.
Patients with DKD who become pregnant should be referred to high-risk obstetrics for evaluation.
